sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.

sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

# Sam's global rules

Prefer the simplest change that works. Challenge me when the evidence points elsewhere. Fail clearly rather than recover, unless recovery was asked for.

## Credentials / Secrets
- For any credential use, or any file that may hold secrets, read the `1password` skill first. Run secret-consuming commands through masked `op run`; keep values out of tool output, command literals, prompts, and saved files.
- Never print stored credentials (`gh auth token`, `--show-token`, `op read` to stdout).
- Secrets come from the 1Password vault `Yolo Sam` with a read-only token. Never mint or self-provision a credential; ask me for a scoped key. A missing one is usually missing on purpose.
- `gh` exception, including to the `1password` skill: use its existing stored login directly; no `op run` or 1Password reference is required. Never extract the token or enable credential-bearing debug output. If authentication fails, ask Sam.
- Never use the paid Anthropic API directly unless Sam explicitly approves the exact task.

## Irreversible
- Delete with `trash`, never `rm`, and only after I approve the exact command.
- Never work in a repo's primary clone; other agents share it. Fresh worktree off `origin/main`, draft PR, `pr-adversarial-review` at its risk-proportional depth, never self-merge. Exception: `~/Projects/obsidian` vault content follows the vault's `AGENTS.md`.

## Conventions
- Plans in `.agents/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-name.md`, claims marked verified or assumed.
- After a correction from me that you accept, run `log-learning`.
- Installs: `pnpm`, `uv`. Wrappers on `PATH` enforce the policy; don't bypass them.
- Browser: `agent-browser`. The full skill list is in `skill-map`; check it before saying a capability is missing.
- Herdr: read the `herdr` skill before controlling panes. For every pane you open, record its returned pane ID and give it a useful name describing its purpose; update the recorded ID if it moves. Before sending input or closing a pane, inspect live state to confirm the ID still identifies your intended pane and process. When finished, close the panes you opened by explicit ID, unless Sam asked to keep them open; never rely on UI focus or close someone else's pane.
- Anything I must paste elsewhere goes on my clipboard via `pbcopy <<'EOF'`.
- To get my decision while I'm away, page me on AgentPager as @~/.agents/agentpager.md says; skip this where that file is missing.
- Machines: `air` (portable laptop), `pro` (desk laptop), `mini` (headless, `ssh mini`, keychain locked over SSH), `neo`.

# Working in this repository

AgentPager brings an agent's decisions to its owner's phone. Its product contract is the Blueprint in `packages/blueprint/`.

Read down the ladder before you judge or change anything:
1. the strategy, `packages/blueprint/strategy/STRATEGY.md`;
2. the promises in `packages/blueprint/design/`: capabilities, invariants, metrics, dependencies and journeys;
3. the design code, and the design catalogue in `packages/blueprint/design/screens/`: the real app's screens and journeys as images and text, to read without a Simulator.

The roadmap, `packages/blueprint/roadmap/ROADMAP.md`, says what is next.

**Current state (31 Oct 2026).** v2 is live: the owner makes pagers on the phone, and agents connect with a pager number through the `agentpager` binary. The Blueprint describes v2: its strategy, terms, capabilities, invariants, journeys and roadmap (`DEC-2026-10-30-v2-promises`). A promise that isn't built yet says "Not built yet"; don't take it as shipped. `docs/v2/` holds the decisions behind it, and `docs/v2/03-binary-surface.md` is what agents see. The phone's design is the SwiftUI app; the catalogue shows each of its screens (`DEC-2026-10-30-screens-from-the-app`). One part still shows v1: the front page's copy. Don't build to what v2 retired: link, QR and emoji pairing, sessions with end times, emoji cards, the web app, the hosted MCP and `recipe.json`.

The Blueprint process lives in [exocognito/blueprint](https://github.com/exocognito/blueprint): start at [src/process/README.md](https://github.com/exocognito/blueprint/blob/main/src/process/README.md). The [law](https://github.com/exocognito/blueprint/blob/main/src/process/law.md) is the rulebook, and [files](https://github.com/exocognito/blueprint/blob/main/src/process/files.md) gives each file's shape.

- Work in an isolated worktree off `origin/main`, and preserve other agents' and the owner's edits.
- Open changes as draft pull requests. The owner merges.
- Install with pnpm. Use Node 22.19 or newer.
- Before handing off a change, run `pnpm check` and `pnpm test:all`, which runs every suite: the design, the server and the binary. `pnpm check` fails when the iPhone app, its UI tests, the brief fixtures, the wire contract or the front page changed without `pnpm designs`, which remakes the catalogue on a Mac with Xcode.

</project_instructions>

# Blueprint files

The folder, the ids and the shape of each file. [The law](law.md) says which layer a file sits in and who writes it.

The driver checks milestone and promise ids and selection status; it does not lint the whole Blueprint. A reviewer reads a Blueprint pull request against the law and this page.

Write each prose paragraph on one source line and let the editor or viewer wrap it. Keep structural newlines in lists, tables, frontmatter and code blocks.

## The folder

```text
<product>/                          a pnpm workspace
  recipe.json                       how the loop runs this product; see simple-loop.md
  packages/blueprint/               one package; the app imports the design from it
    strategy/STRATEGY.md
    design/
      terms.md
      capabilities/C1-slug.md
      invariants/I1-slug.md
      metrics/K1-slug.md
      dependencies/D1-slug.md
      journeys/J1-slug.md
      schemas/                      Effect Schema
      machines/                     xstate v5
      effects/                      typed operations and service tags; the routes and tools, the one list of ways in
      ui/                           screens, fixtures and stories
    verification/                   derived checks of the promises and design, reviewed before pinning
      tla/                          TLA+ models, TLC configurations and design replays
      closure/                      deductive rules and their input derivation
    roadmap/
      ROADMAP.md
      milestones/MSTART.md
    records/
      decisions/DEC-2026-09-13-slug.md
      evidence/RUN-2026-09-13-slug.md   a dated verdict that a metric names
      research/
      workshop/                         notes and canvases from before the package
      lessons/L1-slug.md                what a run taught; the owner says at each pin whether lessons ship
  packages/storybook/               design preview and story-test harness, when needed
  packages/app/                     the product, derived from the pinned Blueprint
    src/                            application implementation, including timing profiles
    test/                           real-product acceptance tests
    test-support/                   shared test setup, profile and corpus selection
    operator/                       app deployment and preparation tools, when needed
```

The Blueprint package holds the reviewed inputs to a build: strategy, promises, design and verification of those promises and design. Verification is derived from the higher layers even though it is pinned with them. App implementation, timing profiles, test support and tests or adapters that replay the models against the real product live in `packages/app/`. Pre-pin verification results live in `packages/blueprint/records/evidence/`; results produced during a run live in the run record. The builder creates `packages/app/` during the first milestone; a later pin may carry the accepted app. Add optional app directories only when the product needs them. Locating a tool under `app/operator/` does not authorize the builder or reviewer to perform operator-only deployment preparation.

## Ids

| Kind | Shape |
| --- | --- |
| Strategy item | `SG1`, `SP1` |
| Capability, invariant, metric, dependency, journey | `C1::pair-a-phone-by-qr`: the id, two colons, a slug. The file is `C1-pair-a-phone-by-qr.md` and its frontmatter `id` is the full form. |
| Milestone | `MSTART`: short, upper case; the file is named by it |
| Decision, evidence record, lesson | `DEC-2026-09-13-slug`, `RUN-2026-09-13-slug`, `L1::slug` |

An id is unique across the product and never reused, including after retirement. A rewording keeps its id. A change of meaning deprecates the old item in place and gives the new meaning a new id. `was:` keeps an old id through a move.

Frontmatter holds identifiers, references and machine-compared values: `id`, `serves`, `for`, `providedBy`, `method`, numeric measurement settings and lifecycle metadata. Sentences belong in the body under headings. Promise and milestone frontmatter uses YAML scalars and block lists, one `- item` per line; those reference lists keep YAML syntax, not Markdown numbering. The shared strategy and terms files may also use the per-entry metadata map below; the driver does not read that map.

## Status

Promises, strategy items and terms have one lifecycle status. Missing `status` means `active`; only non-default values need writing. An explicitly empty or unknown value is invalid. The default is a format convention, not a substitute for the owner's approval.

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `active` | Approved and in force. |
| `draft` | Proposed, awaiting owner approval. |
| `deprecated` | Retired, retained for reference; its identity is never reused. |

A deprecated item also has `successor: <reference> | none` and `decision: DEC-YYYY-MM-DD-slug`. `none` explicitly means no successor; an absent field is an error. The decision resolves under `records/decisions/` and holds the retirement rationale. Do not keep a `Deprecated.` status sentence in the promise body. Retain the former statement and requirements as history, visibly marked by the status. Promise successors use full `ID::slug` references; strategy successors use the strategy id, and term successors use the exact term name.

```yaml
id: D4::sandbox-runtime
status: deprecated
successor: none
decision: DEC-2026-10-12-agent-runs
```

`STRATEGY.md` and `terms.md` each hold several entries. An optional `items` map in their file frontmatter stores metadata by strategy id or exact term name (without Markdown formatting). Omitted entries default to active. The map does not change the headings, definitions or ids; a key with no corresponding entry is invalid. A file-wide status does not stand in for per-entry status. Quote term keys when YAML requires it.

```yaml
items:
  SG2:
    status: draft
  SP3:
    status: deprecated
    successor: SP4
    decision: DEC-2026-10-15-new-principle
```

The same map in `terms.md` may use a key such as `"Read link"` instead of `SG2`. Terms without ids retain their exact name as their identity; a retired name is not reassigned to a different meaning.

Pre-pin review and deductive closure treat an active item's normative citation of or dependency on a deprecated item as a question for the owner. A deprecated item's missing successor target or a successor that is itself deprecated is also a question; `none` is an intentional absence, not a missing target. Historical mentions in decision records do not put retired requirements back in force. A milestone selecting a draft or deprecated promise is broken. Check all entries, not just the next milestone, and check retirement metadata and decision targets. The driver enforces the selected packet's eligibility; the sharpen review covers the remaining relationships.

Readers show every item's effective status beside its metadata, even when defaulted. Put deprecated entries last within their section, with a distinctly colored badge labeled `Deprecated`, and show successor and decision under the title. Keep draft entries visibly labeled too. Color alone is insufficient. This is the rendering contract for Blueprint readers; plain source files keep their ordinary headings and ordering.

## Item references

Every prose list in a promise is numbered from 1, with explicit consecutive source numbers. Use one main list per kind and restart numbering for each heading. Keep supporting requirements in numbered items; code and examples may support an item. Do not use nested prose lists or restart a second list under the same heading, since that makes addresses ambiguous.

An item reference is `<full-id>#<heading-slug>-<number>`: `C5::share-a-view-link#behaviors-2`, `I6::your-run-reaches-only-your-agent#clauses-3`, `J2::a-full-history#preconditions-1`. Use the selected format’s heading consistently (`Behaviors`, `Clauses` or `Obligations`), and use its lowercase words joined by hyphens. Refer to the whole statement as `#statement` and a metric’s complete prose threshold as `#bar` (for example, `K1::save-latency#bar`). These two section addresses resolve the unique named section rather than a numbered item; missing or duplicate sections are invalid. Use these references in current design, review and verification rather than `b2`, `clause3` or a bare number. Milestone `deliverables` and journey `for` still select whole promises, without fragments.

These are logical source addresses. Ordinary Markdown anchors a heading, not each numbered item: a reader offering clickable item links must emit the matching item anchors itself. Do not assume a GitHub link ending in `#behaviors-2` resolves without such rendering. Numbered addresses identify items at a revision, not permanent identities. Update live references when inserting or reordering items; evidence and historical review cite the source revision as well as the item. Do not rewrite old evidence to pretend it checked a new revision.

### Typed relation metadata

Keep relation metadata beside the design or story it describes, for example `design/ui/screens/PageScreen.relations.ts` and `design/machines/page.relations.ts`. A relation has `kind`, `from`, `to` and `scope`; [the law](law.md#design-relations) defines their meaning. For `depicts`, `checks` and `enforces`, `from` is a package-relative source `path` plus a resolvable `locator`, and `to` is the full promise item address (or its revision-qualified form below). An `explains` relation connects a record source to the source it explains. Reuse existing state tags and exports where they identify the source; do not introduce another requirement registry.

```ts
{
  kind: "depicts",
  from: { path: "design/ui/screens/PageScreen.stories.tsx", locator: "export const Saving" },
  to: "C1::new-page-at-once#behaviors-2",
  scope: "Saving indicator and title only; not persistence or leaving safely.",
}
```

Within a snapshot, logical addresses acquire that viewer build's exact full Git revision. The build identifies the repository and revision and resolves both endpoints against that snapshot; dirty working previews must be labeled unpinned and cannot supply approval or historical evidence. A historical link instead carries an explicit immutable revision for each endpoint outside the current snapshot. Never resolve an old promise against a new component. Readers reject unresolved or ambiguous targets and preserve the relation's kind and scope when navigating.

# AgentPager

## Vision

AgentPager makes it easy for me to leave my agents working on my computer or in a cloud VM and send owner decisions to my phone so they can continue to do useful work while I am away. It is an app on my phone that pages me when an agent needs me, the way a pager would.

## Hero Features
_Technically: strategic capabilities_

### SC1 · Unblock my agent from my phone

I make pagers on my phone, as many as I like: one for my AGENTS.md, one for a throwaway VM, one per shared project. Each has a number. An agent I give the number to connects with the agentpager command, and appears on that pager with nothing for me to tap. Every connect is a new agent, shown by who asked (Claude Code, Codex) and grouped by project.

When it needs me, my agent sends a decision: the question first, two to four options, its recommendation, and the detail one tap away. I answer, see that my answer was sent, then get the agent's acknowledgement and next steps. I can look back at an agent's decisions until its pager is deleted, or until it has been idle 30 days.

An option can show exactly what it would send or change, such as a draft email or a diff, so I approve that exact version. The agent carries out the option I chose; AgentPager only carries my answer.

### SC2 · Get paged when my agent needs me

When my agent asks, my phone alerts me with who asked, the project and the question, even when AgentPager is closed and, if I let its alerts through, a Focus mode is on. Opening the alert takes me to that decision. If no agent picks up my answer within 3 minutes, I'm told once, by an alert and on the decision.

## Guarantees
_Technically, SI: a strategic selection of Invariants_

### SI1 · Sending a decision requires confirmation

Following good UX practice, an action that cannot be undone needs a confirming step. So an answer always takes two taps: I choose an option or write a response, then press Send, and I have a few seconds to undo. Choosing alone never sends. The agent receives exactly what I sent.

### SI2 · Only agents I give a number reach my phone

A pager number is an address I give to agents I trust. Whoever has it can send me decisions until I turn that pager off, and can read nothing. I can turn any pager off, and then nothing from it gets through. If a number leaks, I make a new pager rather than turning the old one back on.

### SI3 · Sent decisions cannot be changed

I can reread the question, my answer and the agent's acknowledgement, but not change them.

### SI4 · An acknowledgement always comes from the agent

An acknowledgement is a real message from the agent, never an automatic message from AgentPager. The phone tells apart "your answer was sent", "your agent received it" and "no agent has picked it up".

### SI5 · A pager is on until I turn it off

content.text:
Within a snapshot, logical addresses acquire that viewer build's exact full Git revision. The build identifies the repository and revision and resolves both endpoints against that snapshot; dirty working previews must be labeled unpinned and cannot supply approval or historical evidence. A historical link instead carries an explicit immutable revision for each endpoint outside the current snapshot. Never resolve an old promise against a new component. Readers reject unresolved or ambiguous targets and preserve the relation's kind and scope when navigating.

Historical source endpoints use `{ path, locator, revision }`; historical promise endpoints use `{ address: "<full-id>#<item>", revision: "<full-commit-sha>" }`. The `revision` is optional on a source endpoint: omitted means the current snapshot. A plain promise address also means the current snapshot. Explicit revisions are full immutable Git commit ids in the build's declared repository, never branch names; preserve those commits under durable refs. Both endpoints may specify different revisions only when the relation intentionally documents that historical connection. Historical endpoint resolution is a reader contract to implement and validate; the bounded same-snapshot example does not claim to support it yet.

The viewer derives its index from canonical text and co-located links, not a handwritten requirement map. Quotes, descriptions and historical prototype comparison annotations are explanations, not competing requirements or proof status. The declaration of a check and evidence of its execution are separate; recorded results name their checked inputs and scope under [evidence](evidence.md#blueprint-verification).

## Strategy

`strategy/STRATEGY.md` is one file. Every item below the vision has an id and a heading.

| Part | Id | What it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Vision | none | Why this matters, who it is for and where it is going. |
| Strategic goals | `SG` | What we will achieve, seen only by watching the product in use over time. |
| Strategic principles | `SP` | Stances for deciding when no fact settles it, taste among them. |

Strategy quotes the owner's own phrases wherever they carry taste or intent that a fresh reader would not get from the promises. It does not list what the product does or never does: each capability and invariant is stated once, in its promise file, and the owner approves that statement. A Blueprint written before this rule may still hold strategic capabilities (`SC`) and invariants (`SI`); they are retired, never reused, when its strategy is next rewritten.

## Promises

One file per promise. A journey's shape is [below](#journeys).

```markdown
---
id: I16::confirm-before-binding
serves:
  - SP2
---

## Statement

An account is never connected without you saying yes.

## Clauses

1. Binding an account requires your explicit confirmation.

## Caveats

1. The proof tries the paths the machine has today.
```

`serves` lists the strategy goals and principles that are a capability's, invariant's or metric's reason, where any is. It may be empty. Every promise has a prose `## Statement`, its main numbered list and a numbered `## Caveats` list of proof gaps. If no gaps are recorded, write `None recorded.` under Caveats; that is not a claim of complete proof.

| Kind | Main list | Other sections |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Capability | `## Behaviors`: what a person observes, from a way in. | Optional `## Never` for a specific boundary a builder could plausibly cross; a prohibition across capabilities is an invariant. |
| Invariant | `## Clauses`: one checkable sentence per item explaining what always holds or never happens, and what breaking it looks like. | Its statement is judged true or false without reading code. |
| Journey | `## Steps`: the ordered walk across promises. | See [journeys](#journeys). |
| Dependency | `## Provided`: the external thing the product stands on and did not build, where it is and what it must supply, in words a builder can act on. | `## Never` for prohibitions; `## Proof runs on` for targets, clients, screen sizes and conditions. It holds no secret. |
| Metric | `## Probe`: the numbered measurement procedure and evaluation criteria. | `## Bar` for the prose acceptance threshold. No separate rubric. |

Capabilities and invariants may use `## Obligations` as their main numbered list instead of Behaviors or Clauses. Keep one required list, not parallel restatements. Each obligation states a precise required outcome or prohibition; mechanisms, formal properties, test plans and results bind to that item rather than becoming additional promise requirements merely by appearing in a viewer. Existing formats remain valid; migrate them deliberately and update current references. An obligation is an item in its promise, not another canonical file kind or registry. Its address is, for example, `C7::write-and-return#obligations-2` at an exact revision.

With this format, the Statement is a short, high-level product summary. Each obligation must answer an expectation visible in that summary, while keeping detailed conditions and bounds in the obligation. The owner reviews both. Review in both directions: every summary expectation has required coverage, and every obligation has an owner-relevant reason in the summary. As an omission check, remove each distinct requirement in turn and describe a counterexample to the summary that the remaining requirements would permit. If another selected promise already supplies that requirement, record the shared dependency rather than inventing an independent gap. A missing citation and a missing requirement are different findings. Record this reasoning in the review record; it is a semantic review exercise, not proof of completeness or mechanical deduction from prose.

The summary-to-required-items review applies to every promise kind, not only capabilities and invariants. Preserve each kind's semantics and canonical sections:

| Kind | Precise items the summary leads the owner to review | What the graph binds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| C / I | Obligations (or existing Behaviors / Clauses). | Required outcomes and prohibitions to depictions, enforcement mechanisms and checks. |
| K — metric | Probe plus Bar: population, observation procedure, time window and acceptance threshold as applicable. | Measurement implementation, evaluation and results. A passing sample is not a guarantee for every future observation. |
| D — dependency | Provided, plus any Never and Proof runs on items. | Required external guarantees or assumptions, integration checks and target conditions. The product can check its use and handling of failures; it cannot claim to enforce a provider's availability by construction. |
| J — journey | Ordered Steps with their referenced promises and any journey-specific required outcome. | The cross-promise walk, depicted states, integration checks and results. Reuse referenced requirements; do not copy every C/I obligation into the journey. |

“Obligation” in the review graph means a required item or condition from its canonical promise, not a mandate to rename every section to Obligations. Retain the source kind and exact item address, including a metric's Bar where applicable. The reciprocal review checks all selected required items and shared dependencies; it does not presume that each numbered procedural step is an independent product promise. Terms define vocabulary and strategy gives direction; neither gains an obligation list merely to appear in the graph. Select applicable K/D/J promises for each milestone; showing only C/I in a bounded example is not an exemption.

Any kind may add an optional `## Preconditions` numbered list stating the existing state, scope or setup required before its main list applies. Omit it when unnecessary. Do not use item 0. Moving an existing condition here must preserve its scope: a condition of just one behavior stays in that behavior, not a section that restricts the whole promise. A precondition must not silently weaken the Statement.

A proof choice the owner cares about belongs in the relevant numbered list or Caveats. Where proof runs belongs in a dependency. A choice that cannot be stated as something observable is the reviewer's to make. Metrics keep `method: probe | evidence`, `staleAfterDays` and, when measuring a span, `periodDays` in frontmatter. Dependencies replace `serves` with `providedBy: owner | builder | recipe`. Prose `statement`, `caveats`, `provided` and `bar` fields are replaced by their body headings; legacy prose fields such as `gap` move under their own heading too.

An owner-required timing policy belongs in an invariant: for example, one profile selection makes every product timer in dev one tenth of its prod duration, preserves their order, and keeps production performance bars unchanged. State the scope and any exceptions there. The builder supplies the timing module and test helpers in `packages/app/`; the Blueprint does not prescribe their filenames.

## Design

| Part | Form | Checked in the recipe's setup |
| --- | --- | --- |

statement: A pager turns off only when its owner turns it off or its auto-off comes due, and on only when its owner turns it on. The service forgets a deleted pager with its agents, and an agent with no activity for 30 days.

---

**What turns a pager off.** Its owner's switch, or its auto-off: never, or 24 hours, 7 days or 30 days after it was last turned on (C22). Auto-off lands in the same off state as the switch, off since the time it was due. Nothing else turns a pager off or on, and no activity puts off its auto-off.

**While it is off.** Every call from its agents that sends or collects something (asking, waiting for an answer, acknowledging, finishing), every connect with its number and every answer from its phone is refused with "This pager is turned off. Your message was not delivered." Nothing is queued: nothing refused arrives later. An agent can still ask whether its pager is on. The phone still reads the pager and every decision with its attachments, and turning the pager on makes the open ones answerable again.

**When it is deleted.** The service deletes the pager, its agents, and their decisions, attachments, answers, acknowledgements and key digests. Its number connects nothing, and its agents' keys are refused as unknown.

**Housekeeping.** An agent with no activity for 30 days is forgotten in the same way, and its pager stops listing it. Activity is asking, the owner's answer, acknowledging and finishing; waiting for an answer is not.

**Breaking this looks like:**
1. a decision, answer or acknowledgement that gets through while its pager is off, or arrives once it is turned on again;
2. a pager that turns off or on by any means but its owner and its auto-off;
3. anything the service can still serve from a deleted pager.

## Principles
_Technically SK: a set of strategic metrics (rubrics) that apply to all internal decisions_

### SP1 · Make the usual answer easy and clear

Use plain language I can understand without specialist knowledge. Options are different ways to get the job done. Asking for changes is always there when no option fits; it is the fallback, never an option. In the app, I make pagers, agents connect to them, and I turn a pager off. Nothing is called a session.

### SP2 · Keep the first version focused and its foundations explicit

My side is a native iPhone app. No accounts and no paid plans. It runs on a Cloudflare Worker at agentpager.me, with one Durable Object for the pagers and one per agent. Agents reach it only through the agentpager command, as a command line or a local MCP server. The code is open: anyone can read it, fork it and run their own (*not built yet*).

### SP3 · Agents choose the options; AgentPager keeps them easy to answer

For every card, the agent chooses the question, two to five options and their emoji. Each option is its emoji and title; the emoji, never a number, tells options apart, so I can refer to them when I ask for changes, such as "do 🚀 and then 🛠️". I choose one option, never several, and the phone marks my choice the platform's usual way. On a product card the options are the actions the agent offers, such as Send now or Send tomorrow.

### SP4 · Keep the decision short; make detail optional

Aim for about 100 characters for the question and for each option. The agent may mark the option it recommends; the phone tags it, and nothing is chosen for me. Each option may carry about 200 characters of detail, always shown with it. These are writing guides; SI6 sets the hard limits.

### SP5 · Reach the agents owners actually use

Any agent that can run the agentpager command can use AgentPager: terminal agents, and desktop apps like Claude Desktop and Cursor. Cloud sessions with a shell should work too, untested so far. Agents with no machine of their own, like claude.ai in a browser, are out. The command sets itself up in the agent apps it finds. A waiting agent has my answer within a second of the Undo window closing, with nothing for me to nudge.

### SP6 · Feel native

Use the platform's own components and conventions (lists, sheets, menus, alerts and notifications) rather than custom ones, so the app is familiar and the system does the work.

### SP7 · Letters tell options apart; ✶ marks the recommendation

For every card, the agent chooses the question and two to four options. They are lettered A to D in the order the agent gives them, and the letter tells them apart, so I can refer to them when I ask for changes, such as "do A, then B". I choose one option, never several, and the phone marks my choice the platform's usual way. The agent may mark the option it recommends; the phone marks it ✶, and nothing is chosen for me.

### SP8 · Lead with the decision; keep the rest one tap away

A decision opens on what I need to decide: the question, its context, each option's short label and the agent's recommendation. What each option changes, why to choose or pass on it, what it assumes, the tradeoffs and any attachments stay one tap away. These are writing guides; SI6 sets the hard limits.

# AgentPager

Bring an agent's decisions to the owner's phone. The [strategy](packages/blueprint/strategy/STRATEGY.md), [executable design](packages/blueprint/design/) with its [journeys](packages/blueprint/design/journeys/) and [wire contract](packages/blueprint/design/schemas/exchange.ts), and the [roadmap](packages/blueprint/roadmap/ROADMAP.md) are the product contract. The [workshop](packages/blueprint/records/workshop/) that preceded them is history: `strategy.md` there was promoted into the package with the edits `DEC-2026-09-25-mstart-scope` records, the tldraw board holds the round 3 proposal, and the visual workshop's variant E is the history behind the screens. The apps own appearance, and the [design catalogue](packages/blueprint/design/screens/README.md) records it.

MCARDS, the first milestone, created `packages/app/` from this contract in a cleanroom run using [recipe.json](recipe.json). That recipe is retired with v2: it still targets the retired hosted MCP, so don't run it (`docs/v2/06-blueprint-update-plan.md`). `design/` is the one design folder. Alchemy is deferred by SP2.

## Layout

| Path | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `package.json`, `pnpm-workspace.yaml`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, `tsconfig.json` | The pnpm workspace. Root scripts only delegate to the packages. |
| `recipe.json` | The MCARDS cleanroom run's host, tools, setup and test command. Retired with v2; don't run it. |
| `packages/blueprint/` | The contract, the design code with its unit tests, the design catalogue (`design/screens/`) and the records. |
| `packages/ios/` | The SwiftUI iPhone app, its UI tests and the Xcode project. |
| `packages/app/` | Created by a run: the Worker, client, deploy and dogfood scripts and acceptance tests. The root scripts delegate to it by name. |

## See the design

The design is the real app. The [design catalogue](packages/blueprint/design/screens/README.md) in `packages/blueprint/design/screens/` holds its screens as images and text: every iPhone screen state with its accessibility tree, the main interactions as storyboards of numbered frames with the action between them, and the front page at 390 and 1280 px. Reading it needs nothing installed.

Use Node 22.19 or newer and pnpm. From this directory:

```sh
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm check
pnpm test
```

`pnpm designs` regenerates the catalogue on a Mac with Xcode and the iPhone 17e Simulator: it starts a local server, runs the iPhone UI tests against it and renders the front page in headless Chromium. If Chromium is missing, run `pnpm --filter @agentpager/app exec playwright install chromium`. `pnpm check` fails when anything the catalogue is drawn from (the iPhone app, its UI tests, the brief fixtures, the wire contract or the front page) changed since it was made; run `pnpm designs` and commit the result.

# Running the next roadmap with an orchestrator

How Sam works with one orchestrator agent that runs MENCRYPT, MINSTALL and MSITE in parallel, then MOPEN and MFRIENDS, and asks Sam only at design gates and walks. The roadmap and milestones are in `packages/blueprint/roadmap/`; the decision is `DEC-2026-10-31-next-roadmap`.

## Shape

- **One orchestrator**, a long-lived Claude Code session in Herdr with its own agentpager agent id. It owns the roadmap, starts and briefs the leads, sequences merges, deploys, and is the only agent that pages Sam about the roadmap as a whole.
- **One lead per milestone**, in its own worktree off `origin/main` and its own Herdr pane. A lead turns its milestone's "Sam decides first" list into one pager card, writes the promise changes, builds in PR-sized slices and runs `pr-adversarial-review` on each PR.
- **Reviewers** are started by each lead, as the skill says. MENCRYPT's PRs take the adversarial loop, since they cross the trust boundary and change stored data. Most MSITE PRs take a sanity check.

The Blueprint's own simple loop (builder and reviewer in a cleanroom VM) isn't used: AgentPager's recipe is retired with v2 (README), and this week's work ran as worktrees and PRs (verified).

## Where Sam comes in

| Milestone | Before building | During | At the end |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| MENCRYPT | One card: the two switch-over questions | Nothing expected | Walk on the phone |
| MINSTALL | One card: download host, machines, update path, demo agent | Sam's own App Store Connect steps: the TestFlight app, the Beta App Review submission. Agents never sign or hold Apple credentials (D6, D7) | Install from a TestFlight link and the one line, on a clean machine |
| MSITE | Workshop round 1: who it's for and what it must say | Round 2, structure; round 3, how it looks. Each round is published as real pages to look at on the phone, and Sam answers by comments or a card | Look at the live page |
| MOPEN | One card: licence, home, history, alerts for self-hosters, what goes | Reading the public repository before it goes public. Publishing can't be undone | Fork and self-host guide read-through |
| MFRIENDS | Who to invite, and how feedback comes back | Sam's own invitations | Sam's call on what changes next |

Each card carries the lead's recommendation, so a gate can be one tap. An answer the lead can't act on goes back to the orchestrator, not straight to Sam again.

## Rules that keep parallel work from colliding

- **Owners of shared files.** MENCRYPT owns the wire contract (`packages/blueprint/design/schemas/`), the Agent object's storage and the command's send path. MINSTALL owns the command's build and release scripts and the install endpoint. MSITE owns the front page (`MarketingScreen.tsx`, `marketing.css`) and `/start`'s words. A lead that needs another's file asks the orchestrator.
- **The iPhone project file.** MENCRYPT adds a notification service extension and an App Group, and MINSTALL changes signing and the push environment. Both edit `project.pbxproj`, so the orchestrator merges one, then has the other rebase.
- **The switch-over waits for the update path.** MENCRYPT's refusal of commands from before encryption ships only once MINSTALL's install line can update them.
- **One Simulator run at a time.** `pnpm designs` takes the iPhone 17e Simulator for about 12 minutes and rewrites the catalogue, so the orchestrator runs it for one PR at a time (verified: 12 min on the last run).
- **Only the orchestrator deploys**, from `main` after a merge, the service before the binaries (D1).
- **MOPEN's cleanup starts after MENCRYPT merges.** Its decisions and a secrets audit can start at once.

## Keeping Sam informed

The orchestrator pages Sam only for gates and walks. For everything else, Sam can read the Blueprint page, regenerated from `main` after each merge (assumed: needs `pnpm blueprint:page`, not built yet).

## To start

1. Sam merges the roadmap PR.
2. The orchestrator sends three cards: MENCRYPT's switch-over, MINSTALL's decisions, and MSITE's first workshop brief.
3. It starts three leads as the answers arrive. MENCRYPT can start building at once, since its questions only shape the switch-over at the end.
